stimuli.text: The temperature of a liquid, in degrees Celsius, is modeled by a differentiable function $$H$$ of time $$t$$, in minutes. Selected values are shown.
The function $$f$$ is defined for all real numbers except $$x = 2$$. Selected values of $$f$$ are shown.
The graph of $$f'$$, the derivative of a function $$f$$, consists of line segments on $$0 \leq x \leq 6$$, as shown.

image.alt: Graph of f′: line segments through the points (0, -2), (1, 0), (2, -2), (3, 1), (4, -2), (5, 3), (6, 2).

stimuli.text: The function $$f$$ is continuous on the closed interval $$[0, 4]$$. Selected values of $$f$$ are shown in the table.
The function $$g$$ is differentiable. Selected values of $$g$$ are shown.
A slope field for a differential equation is shown at the points with integer coordinates.

image.alt: A slope field drawn on the grid from x = -2 to 2 and y = -2 to 2.

stimuli.text: Let $$R$$ be the region enclosed by the graphs of $$f(x) = 2\cos\left(\frac{x}{2}\right)$$ and $$g(x) = x^2 - 1$$.
A particle moves along the x-axis. Its velocity is given by $$v(t) = 5\sin\left(\frac{t^2}{2}\right) - 1.5$$ for $$0 \leq t \leq 4$$. At time $$t = 0$$ the particle is at position $$x = 3$$.
The continuous function $$f$$ is defined on $$0 \leq x \leq 6$$. Its graph consists of line segments, as shown. Let $$g(x) = \int_{2}^{x} f(t)\,dt$$.
People enter an amusement park at a rate modeled by a differentiable function $$P$$, where $$P(t)$$ is measured in people per minute and $$t$$ is measured in minutes. Selected values are shown.
Consider the differential equation $$\frac{dy}{dx} = 4x(y + 1)$$. Let $$y = f(x)$$ be the particular solution with $$f(1) = 0$$.

questions.stem: What is the average rate of change of $$H$$ over the interval $$5 \leq t \leq 10$$, in degrees Celsius per minute?

options.why: This is the average temperature, not the average rate of change.
This is the total change in temperature; it still needs to be divided by the elapsed time.
This divides time by temperature, which is upside down.

questions.explanation: Average rate of change $$= \frac{H(10) - H(5)}{10 - 5} = \frac{23 - 60}{5} = -\frac{37}{5}$$ degrees per minute.

questions.stem: Based on the table, which of the following is the best estimate of $$\lim_{x \to 2} f(x)$$?

options.why: This is only the right-hand trend.
Averaging the two sides is never how a limit is found.
Correct. From the left the outputs approach -3; from the right they approach -5. The one-sided limits differ.
This is only the left-hand trend.

questions.explanation: Read the table toward $$x = 2$$ from each side. The left side approaches -3 and the right side approaches -5, so the two-sided limit does not exist.

options.why: This differentiates the outer power but leaves out the derivative of the inside function.
This is the value of the function, not its derivative.
This applies the power rule to the derivative of the inside instead of to the inside function.

questions.stem: A twice-differentiable function $$f$$ satisfies $$f'(2) = 0$$ and $$f''(2) = 0$$. Which of the following must be true?

options.why: $$x^4$$ has a minimum, but $$-x^4$$ has a maximum with the same conditions.
$$-x^4$$ has a maximum, but $$x^4$$ has a minimum with the same conditions.

options.text: $$f$$ has a point of inflection at $$x = 2$$.
options.why: $$x^3$$ has an inflection point there, but $$x^4$$ does not.

options.text: There is not enough information to classify $$x = 2$$.
options.why: Correct. When f″(c) = 0 the Second Derivative Test is inconclusive: $$x^3$$, $$x^4$$ and $$-x^4$$ all have f′(0) = f″(0) = 0.

questions.explanation: With $$f''(c) = 0$$ the test gives no conclusion. Use the First Derivative Test instead.

questions.stem: What is $$\int_{1}^{4} \left(-3x^{2} + 2x + 5\right)dx$$?

options.why: Correct. An antiderivative is $$F(x) = -x^{3} + x^{2} + 5x$$; $$F(4) - F(1) = -33$$.
This adds F(a) instead of subtracting it.
This is F(b) only; subtract F(a) as well.
This subtracts values of the integrand instead of an antiderivative.

questions.explanation: By the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, $$\int_{1}^{4} f(x)\,dx = F(4) - F(1)$$ with $$F(x) = -x^{3} + x^{2} + 5x$$. That is $$-28 - (5) = -33$$.

questions.stem: What is $$\int_0^{4} \frac{1}{x + 2}\,dx$$?

options.why: This is the ratio minus one, not a logarithm.
This uses a power-rule-style antiderivative; the antiderivative of 1/u is ln|u|.
Correct. $$\ln|x + 2|\Big|_0^{4} = \ln 6 - \ln 2 = \ln 3$$.
This forgets to subtract the value at the lower limit.

questions.explanation: $$\int \frac{dx}{x + 2} = \ln|x + 2| + C$$, so the integral is $$\ln\frac{6}{2} = \ln 3$$.

questions.stem: Let $$f(x) = 2x^{3} - 18x^{2} + 30x$$. At what value of $$x$$ does $$f$$ have a relative minimum?

options.why: This is where f″ = 0 (the inflection point), not a critical point.
$$f(0) = 0$$, but $$f'(0)$$ is not zero, so this is not a critical point.
At this critical point $$f'$$ changes from positive to negative, which gives a relative maximum.
Correct. $$f'(x) = 6(x - 1)(x - 5)$$ changes from negative to positive at $$x = 5$$.

questions.explanation: $$f'(x) = 6x^2 - 36x + 30 = 6(x - 1)(x - 5)$$. Testing signs: $$f'$$ is positive left of $$1$$, negative between $$1$$ and $$5$$, positive right of $$5$$. So there is a relative maximum at $$1$$ and a relative minimum at $$5$$.

questions.stem: If $$f(x) = \csc x$$, what is $$f'\left(\frac{\pi}{6}\right)$$?

options.why: Correct. $$f'(x) = -\csc x \cot x$$, evaluated at $$\frac{\pi}{6}$$.
This value doesn't come from the correct derivative formula.
This mixes up the derivative with a different trigonometric value at the point.
Check the sign: the derivatives of the co-functions (cot, csc) are negative; tan and sec are not.

questions.explanation: $$\frac{d}{dx}\left(\csc x\right) = -\csc x \cot x$$. Substituting $$x = \frac{\pi}{6}$$ gives $$-2\sqrt{3}$$.

questions.stem: Let $$P(t)$$ be the population of a town, in people, at time t years. Which of the following is the best interpretation of $$P'(5) = 8$$?

options.text: The population changes by 8 over the first 5 years.
options.why: This describes a total change over an interval, which is an integral of the rate, not the derivative at one point.

options.text: The population is increasing at a rate of 8 people per year at time $$t = 5$$ years.
options.why: Correct. A derivative at a point is an instantaneous rate of change, with units of output per unit of input.

options.text: The average rate of change of the population over the first 5 years is 8 people per year.
options.why: The derivative is an instantaneous rate at one input, not an average over an interval.

options.text: The population at time $$t = 5$$ years is 8.
options.why: This describes $$P(5)$$, the value of the function, not its rate of change.

questions.explanation: $$P'(5)$$ is the instantaneous rate of change of $$P$$ at time $$t = 5$$ years. Its sign (positive) says the population is increasing, and its units are people per year.

questions.stem: Let $$f(x) = \begin{cases} 3x + 3 & x < 4 \\ -3x + 6 & x \geq 4 \end{cases}$$. What is $$\lim_{x \to 4} f(x)$$?

options.why: Correct. The left-hand limit is $$15$$ and the right-hand limit is $$-6$$. They differ, so the two-sided limit does not exist.
This is $$f(4)$$ and the right-hand limit only. The left-hand limit is $$15$$.
This is the left-hand limit only. The right-hand limit is $$-6$$.
A limit is never the average of the one-sided limits. When they differ, the limit does not exist.

questions.explanation: From the left, $$f(x) = 3x + 3 \to 15$$. From the right, $$f(x) = -3x + 6 \to -6$$. Since $$15 \neq -6$$, $$\lim_{x \to 4} f(x)$$ does not exist.

questions.stem: A quantity $$y$$ satisfies $$\frac{dy}{dt} = ky$$ and doubles every 2 hours. What is the value of $$k$$?

options.why: Doubling means e^{kT} = 2; solve with a logarithm.
Solving $$2k = \ln 2$$ requires dividing by $$2$$.
Correct. $$y = y_0e^{kt}$$ and $$e^{2k} = 2$$.
This is not a solution of e^{kT} = 2.

questions.stem: At what value of $$x$$ does the graph of $$f(x) = -x^{3} - 9x^{2} + x + 5$$ have a point of inflection?

options.why: This is −b/(2a), the vertex formula for a parabola, applied to the cubic's coefficients. Set f″(x) = 0 instead.
Sign error when solving f″(x) = 0.
Correct. $$f''(x) = -6x - 18$$ is zero and changes sign at $$x = -3$$.
Inflection points are where f″ changes sign, not where f″ has its constant term.

questions.explanation: $$f'(x) = -3x^{2} - 18x + 1$$ and $$f''(x) = -6x - 18$$. $$f''$$ is linear, so it changes sign at its zero, $$x = -3$$.

questions.stem: What is $$\lim_{h \to 0} \frac{\ln(6 + h) - \ln 6}{h}$$?

options.why: Correct. This is the derivative of $$\ln x$$ at $$6$$, which is $$\frac{1}{6}$$.
This is the function value, not the derivative.
Substitution gives $$\frac{0}{0}$$, an indeterminate form.
The derivative of $$\ln x$$ is $$\frac{1}{x}$$, not $$x$$.

questions.explanation: By the definition of the derivative, the limit is $$f'(6)$$ for $$f(x) = \ln x$$, so it equals $$\frac{1}{6}$$.

questions.stem: If $$\int_0^{3} f(x)\,dx = -6$$ and $$\int_0^{6} f(x)\,dx = -1$$, what is $$\int_{3}^{6} \left(-3f(x) + 5\right)dx$$?

options.why: The integral of the constant $$5$$ over an interval of length $$3$$ is $$15$$, not $$5$$.
This adds the two given integrals; the integral from a to b is their difference.
This forgets to multiply the integral of $$f$$ by $$-3$$.

questions.explanation: $$\int_{3}^{6} f(x)\,dx = \int_0^{6} f - \int_0^{3} f = 5$$. By linearity, the requested integral is $$-3 \cdot 5 + 5 \cdot 3 = 0$$.

questions.stem: $$\int \left(3x^{2} + 2\cdot\frac{1}{x} + 4e^{x}\right)dx =$$

options.why: After raising the power, divide by the new exponent.
This differentiates instead of antidifferentiating.
The antiderivative of 1/x is ln|x|, not a power of x.
Correct. Raise the power by one and divide by the new power; the antiderivative of 1/x is ln|x|; e^x is its own antiderivative.

questions.explanation: Term by term: $$\int 3x^{2}dx = x^{3}$$, $$\int \frac{2}{x}dx = 2\ln|x|$$, and $$\int 4e^x dx = 4e^x$$. Add the constant of integration.

questions.stem: On the open interval $$0 < x < 6$$, at how many values of $$x$$ does $$f$$ have a relative maximum?

options.why: A relative maximum of f occurs only where f′ changes from positive to negative; touching or crossing upward does not count.
Correct. Count the places where f′ crosses the x-axis from above to below.
A relative maximum of f occurs only where f′ changes from positive to negative; touching or crossing upward does not count.
A relative maximum of f occurs only where f′ changes from positive to negative; touching or crossing upward does not count.

questions.explanation: $$f$$ has a relative maximum where $$f'$$ changes from positive to negative. On this graph that happens 1 time.

questions.stem: If $$f(x) = \arctan(3x)$$, what is $$f'(-1)$$?

options.why: Correct. $$f'(x) = \frac{3}{1 + 9x^2}$$.
This uses $$1 + x^2$$ in the denominator instead of $$1 + (3x)^2$$.
This leaves out the inner derivative $$3$$.
The inside is squared as a whole: $$(3x)^2 = 9x^2$$.

questions.stem: What is the least number of solutions that the equation $$f(x) = 0$$ must have on the interval $$[0, 4]$$?

options.why: This undercounts: each sign change between consecutive values guarantees its own zero.
Correct. The sign of $$f$$ changes 1 time between consecutive table values, and the Intermediate Value Theorem guarantees a zero in each such interval.
The IVT only guarantees zeros where the sign changes; other zeros are possible but not required.
The IVT only guarantees zeros where the sign changes; other zeros are possible but not required.

questions.explanation: Because $$f$$ is continuous, the Intermediate Value Theorem guarantees a solution of $$f(x) = 0$$ on every interval where the values change sign. Counting the sign changes in the table gives 1.

options.why: This multiplies the derivatives of the two factors and then drops the exponential.
This is the derivative of the first factor times the second, without the second term of the product rule.
This differentiates only the exponential factor.

questions.stem: The region bounded by $$y = x^2$$, the x-axis, and the line $$x = 2$$ is revolved about the x-axis. What is the volume of the resulting solid?

options.why: This integrates the radius instead of the radius squared.
$$(x^2)^2 = x^4$$, whose antiderivative is $$\frac{x^5}{5}$$.
The disc method has a factor of $$\pi$$.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the solution to $$\frac{dy}{dx} = 2xy$$ with $$y(0) = 5$$?

options.why: Correct. $$\frac{dy}{y} = 2x\,dx$$ gives $$\ln|y| = x^2 + C$$.
The constant multiplies the exponential; it is not added.
The antiderivative of $$2x$$ is $$x^2$$, not $$2x$$.
This would satisfy dy/dx = 2x, not 2xy.

questions.explanation: $$\int \frac{dy}{y} = \int 2x\,dx$$, so $$\ln|y| = x^2 + C$$ and $$y = Ae^{x^2}$$. $$y(0) = 5$$ gives $$A = 5$$.

questions.stem: The base of a solid is the region bounded by $$y = \sqrt{x}$$, the x-axis, and $$x = 2$$. Cross sections perpendicular to the x-axis are equilateral triangles. What is the volume of the solid?

options.why: This is the volume for cross sections that are squares.
This is the volume for cross sections that are semicircles.
Correct. Each cross section has side $$\sqrt{x}$$, area $$\frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}x$$; integrate from 0 to 2.
This is the volume for cross sections that are isosceles right triangles with a leg in the base.

questions.explanation: The cross section at $x$ has side $$\sqrt{x}$$, area $$\frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}x$$. Integrating from 0 to 2 gives $\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{3}$.

questions.stem: The radius of a circle is increasing at a constant rate of 4 centimeters per second. At the instant when the radius is 6 centimeters, what is the rate of change of the area?

options.why: This leaves out a factor from differentiating the formula with respect to time.
Correct. Differentiate $$A = \pi r^2$$ with respect to $$t$$: $$\frac{dA}{dt} = 2\pi r\frac{dr}{dt}$$.
This forgets to multiply by the given rate of change of the dimension.
This substitutes into the original formula instead of its derivative.

questions.explanation: $$\frac{dA}{dt} = 2\pi r\frac{dr}{dt}$$. Substitute the dimension $$6$$ and its rate $$4$$ to get $$48\pi$$ (cubic or square centimeters per second).

questions.stem: A farmer has 128 meters of fencing to enclose a rectangular field along a straight river. No fence is needed along the river. What is the largest possible area of the field, in square meters?

options.why: This doesn't account for the two equal sides perpendicular to the river.
Correct. With width $$x$$ perpendicular to the river, $$A = x(128 - 2x)$$, maximized at $$x = 32$$.
This fences all four sides (a square), but the river side needs no fence.
This makes all three fenced sides equal, which is not optimal.

questions.explanation: $$A(x) = x(128 - 2x)$$, $$A'(x) = 128 - 4x = 0$$ at $$x = 32$$, and $$A'' = -4 < 0$$, so this is a maximum. The dimensions are $$32$$ by $$64$$, with area $$2048$$.

questions.stem: For the curve $$x^2 + xy + y^2 = 7$$, what is $$\frac{dy}{dx}$$ at the point $$(-2, -1)$$?

options.why: Sign error when solving for dy/dx.
Correct. $$2x + y + x\frac{dy}{dx} + 2y\frac{dy}{dx} = 0$$, so $$\frac{dy}{dx} = -\frac{2x + y}{x + 2y}$$.
This differentiates $$xy$$ as $$y$$, forgetting the product rule term $$x\frac{dy}{dx}$$.
This ignores the $$xy$$ term entirely.

questions.explanation: Implicit differentiation with the product rule on $$xy$$: $$2x + (y + xy') + 2yy' = 0$$. Solving, $$y' = -\frac{2x + y}{x + 2y}$$; at $$(-2, -1)$$, $$y' = -\frac{5}{4}$$.

options.why: Correct. Divide first: $$\frac{3x^{2} + 6}{x} = 3x + \frac{6}{x}$$.
The antiderivative of $$3x$$ is $$\frac{3}{2}x^2$$.
The antiderivative of $$\frac{1}{x}$$ is $$\ln|x|$$.
You cannot integrate a quotient by integrating the top and bottom separately.

questions.explanation: $$\int \left(3x + \frac{6}{x}\right)dx = \frac{3}{2}x^2 + 6\ln|x| + C$$.

questions.stem: What is $$\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\sqrt{x + 4} - 2}{x}$$?

options.why: The expression is undefined at 0, but rationalizing shows the outputs approach a single number.
This forgets that the conjugate denominator is $$\sqrt{x + 4} + 2$$, which approaches $$4$$, not $$2$$.
Correct. Rationalizing gives $$\frac{1}{\sqrt{x + 4} + 2}$$, which approaches $$\frac{1}{4}$$.
Substitution gives $$\frac{0}{0}$$, an indeterminate form.

questions.explanation: Multiply by $$\frac{\sqrt{x + 4} + 2}{\sqrt{x + 4} + 2}$$. The numerator becomes $$x$$, which cancels, leaving $$\frac{1}{\sqrt{x + 4} + 2} \to \frac{1}{4}$$.

questions.stem: Let $$f(x) = x^{3} + 4x + 2$$, and let $$g$$ be the inverse function of $$f$$. What is $$g'(18)$$?

options.why: This evaluates $$f'$$ at $$18$$ instead of at the input $$2$$ with $$f(2) = 18$$.
This takes the reciprocal of a function value, not of the derivative.
This is $$f'(2)$$; the inverse's derivative is its reciprocal.

questions.stem: A particle moves along a line with velocity $$v(t) = 3(t - 2)(t - 6)$$ for $$t \geq 0$$. For which values of $$t$$ is the particle speeding up?

options.why: This is where the velocity is negative, which only means the particle moves left.
Correct. The particle speeds up when velocity and acceleration have the same sign.
On $$0 < t < 2$$ the velocity is positive but the acceleration is negative, so it is slowing down.
This misses $$2 < t < 4$$, where both $$v$$ and $$a$$ are negative.

questions.explanation: $$a(t) = 6t - 24$$ changes sign at $$t = 4$$. $$v$$ is negative on $$(2, 6)$$ and positive elsewhere. Both are negative on $$(2, 4)$$ and both positive for $$t > 6$$.

questions.stem: The region enclosed by $$y = x$$ and $$y = x^2$$ is revolved about the x-axis. What is the volume of the resulting solid?

options.why: This uses only the outer radius (a disc instead of a washer).
This squares the difference of the radii instead of taking the difference of the squares.
Correct. $$\pi\int_0^{1} \left[(x)^2 - (x^2)^2\right]dx$$: outer radius squared minus inner radius squared.
This is π times the area of the region, not a volume of revolution.

questions.stem: Using the data in the table and the values on either side of $$x = 6$$, what is the best estimate of $$g'(6)$$?

options.why: This is the change in g without dividing by the change in x.
This forgets to divide by the change in x.
This divides the output by the input, which is not a rate of change.

questions.explanation: The slope of the secant line through the neighboring points estimates the derivative: $$g'(6) \approx \frac{6 - (12)}{5} = -\frac{6}{5}$$.

questions.stem: What is $$\int_0^{1} x\left(x^2 + 2\right)dx$$?

options.why: After substituting, the limits must change to u-values (from c to 1 + c), not stay 0 to 1.
This evaluates only at the upper limit.
Correct. With $$u = x^2 + 2$$, $$du = 2x\,dx$$, the integral is $$\frac{1}{2}\int_{2}^{3} u\,du$$.
This forgets the factor $$\frac{1}{2}$$ from $$du = 2x\,dx$$.

questions.stem: What is the value of $$\int_{0}^{2} \frac{x}{1 + \cos^2 x}\,dx$$?

options.why: This is the change in the integrand, not the integral.
This integrates over only half of the interval.
This is a single rectangle using the right endpoint, a rough estimate rather than the integral.
Correct. Use the calculator's numerical integration.

questions.explanation: On a graphing calculator, $$\int_{0}^{2} \frac{x}{1 + \cos^2 x}\,dx \approx 1.717$$.

questions.stem: The temperature of a room, in degrees Fahrenheit, is modeled by $$H(t) = 86 + 19\sin\left(\frac{t}{5}\right)e^{-t/20}$$, where $$t$$ is measured in hours. What is the instantaneous rate of change of the temperature at $$t = 13$$, in degrees Fahrenheit per hour?

options.why: This is the temperature itself, not its rate of change.
This multiplies the rate by the time, which is not a rate.
This is the average rate of change over $$0 \leq t \leq 13$$, not the instantaneous rate.
Correct. The calculator's numerical derivative of $$H$$ at $$t = 13$$ gives -1.956; the temperature is decreasing.

questions.explanation: The instantaneous rate of change is $$H'(13) \approx -1.956$$ degrees Fahrenheit per hour, from the calculator's numerical derivative.

questions.stem: A particle moves along a line with velocity $$v(t) = 3\sin(t)\,e^{-t/6} + 0.3$$. What is the total distance the particle travels over $$0 \leq t \leq 5$$?

options.why: Correct. $$\int_0^{5} |v(t)|\,dt$$ on the calculator.
This is the displacement; backward motion subtracts from it.
This is the speed at the final time.
This is the average speed, not the distance.

questions.explanation: Total distance $$= \int_0^{5} |v(t)|\,dt \approx 6.971$$. The displacement $$\int_0^{5} v(t)\,dt \approx 4.262$$ is smaller because the particle moves backward part of the time.

questions.stem: Sand is added to a pile at a rate modeled by $$R(t) = 30 + 4\sin\left(\frac{t}{4}\right)\sqrt{t + 1}$$ cubic feet per hour, for $$0 \leq t \leq 5$$. At time $$t = 0$$ the pile contains 96 cubic feet of sand. How much sand is in the pile at $$t = 5$$?

options.why: This adds the rate at one instant, not the accumulated amount.
This is only the sand added; include the initial amount.
Correct. $$96 + \int_0^{5} R(t)\,dt$$.
This assumes the rate stays at R(T) for the whole time.

questions.explanation: Amount = initial amount + accumulated change = $$96 + \int_0^{5} R(t)\,dt \approx 96 + 172.305 = 268.305$$ cubic feet.

questions.stem: What is the absolute maximum value of $$f(x) = xe^{-x/4} + \frac{\sin x}{4}$$ on the interval $$[0, 6]$$?

options.why: This is where the maximum occurs (the x-value), not the maximum value.
This is the value at the right endpoint, which is not the largest.
This evaluates f at the critical point of the first term alone; the sine term shifts the maximum.
Correct. Graph f on the calculator and find its maximum on the interval, checking the endpoints too.

questions.explanation: On the calculator, the maximum of $$f$$ on $$[0, 6]$$ occurs at $$x \approx 2.502$$, where $$f(x) \approx 1.488$$. The endpoint values are smaller.

questions.stem: A particle moves along the x-axis with velocity $$v(t) = 3\cos\left(\frac{t^2}{5}\right) - 0.5$$ for $$0 \leq t \leq 4$$. At what time does the particle first change direction?

options.why: Correct. The velocity first changes sign at $$t \approx 2.649$$, found by solving $$v(t) = 0$$ on the calculator.
This is a later time; the question asks for the first change of direction.
This is the initial velocity, not a time.
This is an acceleration value, not a time when the velocity changes sign.

questions.explanation: A particle changes direction where $$v(t)$$ changes sign. Graphing $$v$$ on the calculator, the first sign change is at $$t \approx 2.649$$.

questions.stem: Which of the following differential equations could have the slope field shown?

options.why: Test a few points: at some grid points this equation gives a slope with the wrong sign or steepness.
Correct. Check where the segments are horizontal and where the slopes are positive or negative; this equation matches at every point.
Test a few points: at some grid points this equation gives a slope with the wrong sign or steepness.
Test a few points: at some grid points this equation gives a slope with the wrong sign or steepness.

questions.explanation: Compare slopes at specific points. For example, at $$(1, 0)$$ the field's segment has slope $$0$$, and at $$(0, 1)$$ slope $$0$$, which matches $$\frac{dy}{dx} = xy$$.

questions.stem: The function $$g$$ is defined by $$g(x) = \frac{\sin(4x)}{e^{2x} - 1}$$ for $$x \neq 0$$. For what value of $$g(0)$$ is $$g$$ continuous at $$x = 0$$?

options.why: Substitution gives $$\frac{0}{0}$$, which is indeterminate, not 0.
The two small quantities do not shrink at the same rate.
This inverts the ratio.
Correct. Evaluating $$g$$ at inputs very close to 0 (or using the limits of $$\frac{\sin u}{u}$$ and $$\frac{e^u - 1}{u}$$) gives $$\frac{4}{2}$$.

questions.explanation: For continuity, $$g(0)$$ must equal $$\lim_{x \to 0} g(x)$$. Near 0, $$\sin(4x) \approx 4x$$ and $$e^{2x} - 1 \approx 2x$$, so the limit is $$\frac{4}{2} \approx 2.000$$. A table of values near 0 confirms it.

questions.stem: What is the area of the region enclosed by the graphs of $$y = 2\cos\left(\frac{x}{2}\right)$$ and $$y = x^2 - 1$$?

options.why: Correct. The curves meet at $$x \approx -1.557$$ and $$x \approx 1.557$$; integrate top minus bottom.
This is the area under the top curve only.
This adds the absolute values of the curves instead of subtracting.
This is the distance between the intersection points, not an area.

questions.explanation: Store the intersection x-values from the calculator, then $$\int_{-1.557}^{1.557} \left(2\cos\frac{x}{2} - (x^2 - 1)\right)dx \approx 6.215$$.

questions.stem: Consider the curve $$x^2 - xy + y^2 = 48$$, for which $$\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{y - 2x}{2y - x}$$. At which points on the curve is the tangent line horizontal?

options.why: These are the y-intercepts; there the slope is 1/2, not 0.
Correct. Horizontal tangents need $$y - 2x = 0$$. Substituting $$y = 2x$$ gives $$3x^2 = 48$$.
These have 2y − x = 0, where the denominator is zero: the tangent lines are vertical.
These points do not lie on the curve.

questions.stem: Let $$f(x) = x^{3} + 3x + e^{x/3}$$, and let $$g$$ be the inverse of $$f$$. What is the value of $$g'(9)$$?

options.why: This is f′ at the matching input; the inverse's derivative is its reciprocal.
